*Forecasts do not include any estimate for gold sale effect BALANCE OF GOODS AND SERVICES - Estimating the June figures with any confidence is almost impossible since the Bureau of Statistics is including part of the Reserve Bank's sale of gold in the data as an export, and no forecast has been given as a result. The exact sum is not known but the RBA has said some 125 tonnes of gold had been sold forward for June delivery and another 42 tonnes spread over August and September.

Thus should ensure the largest goods surplus on record although analysts are unclear how the sale will be accounted for since the RBA used the funds received to buy foreign bonds of an equal amount, thus implying little net change in reserves.
It was likely the gold sale would boost the net export contribution to GDP, but be exactly martched by a corresponding fall in stocks which would detract from growth.

There was also some uncertainty over the underlying position with some economists expecting a hefty rise in imports of up to 15 percent which would have produced a deficit without the gold impact. Analysts also believed there were planes worth around A$200 million in imports and noted a ship worth A$500 million had inflated exports in May.

BUILDING APPROVALS - This series has also been complicated by the inclusion of the Olympic Village in the May figures which substantially boosted the measure -- excluding this approvals would have fallen around 12 percent instead of rising 2.2 percent. A rise in June, therefore, would imply a substantial bounce back in normal approvals, that is not tied to a special project, of around 1,500 units. Even a modest fall would not be that weak so interpreting the figures will take some tact.

RETAIL SALES - Probably the most important release of the week given the very erratic performance of sales in April and May -- a 1.7 percent fall followed by a 2.9 percent rise -- and the market's obsession with interest rates just now. The wide range of forecasts reflects this volatility as well as uncertainty about the state of consumer demand in general.
Analysts noted vehicle sales were up very strongly in the month -- registrations were at a record high -- and consumer sentiment looked to have improved following the cut in official rates of May 23.

A rise on the month would be a firm result given May's jump but it would have to be strong indeed to make the market re-think its expectation of an official rate cut in the near future. Sale volumes in the quarter should be supported by the very low level of the retail trade deflator, but not be enough to see much a real rise on top of the hefty 2.2 percent gain recorded in Q1.
